summaries.example: Imagine two students tasting the same soup. One says, “It is delicious,” and the other says, “It is too spicy.” A relativist might ask whether “delicious” is true for a particular taster or standard, rather than assuming there must be one answer that is correct for everyone. This does not mean every disagreement disappears; it raises a question about what makes a judgment correct.
summaries.summary: Relativism is a family of philosophical views, not one single idea. It says that some things—such as truth, right and wrong, beauty, or good reasoning—depend on a framework of assessment. The framework might be a person, a culture, a language, a historical period, or a set of beliefs. Relativists often say there is no completely neutral viewpoint outside all frameworks from which we can settle every disagreement. The entry explains several ways to define relativism. One definition looks at what depends on what: for example, justice may depend on local norms. Another defines relativism by contrast with absolutism, objectivism, and the idea that there is only one correct answer. A third says that ordinary claims may hide an unstated phrase such as “according to this standard.” The entry also distinguishes local from global relativism and weak from strong relativism. Supporters connect relativism with cultural diversity, difficult disagreements, and tolerance. Critics worry about self-refutation, communication, rational judgment, and the danger of treating all views as equally acceptable. The central lesson is that different forms of relativism must be examined separately.
key_ideas: Relativism says that some judgments are correct only in relation to a framework or point of view.
A framework might be a person’s preferences, a culture, a language, or a way of thinking.
Some relativists focus on one area, such as taste or morality. This is called local relativism.
Global relativism says that all beliefs or truths are relative, but critics worry that this view may undermine itself.
Relativism is connected with diversity, disagreement, tolerance, and questions about whether there is a neutral way to choose between frameworks.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relativism helps us notice that our judgments may be shaped by habits, language, culture, and standards we do not always notice. That can encourage curiosity and caution before declaring that everyone else is simply wrong. At the same time, the idea creates serious questions: Can people still reason together? Can some beliefs really be better supported than others? Studying these questions helps us discuss differences without confusing respect for people with agreement about every claim.

important_terms.definition: The idea that some truths, values, or standards depend on a person, culture, language, or other framework.
A background point of view or set of rules used to decide what is true, right, beautiful, or reasonable.
The view that at least some truths or values apply everywhere and do not depend on a culture or situation.
The part of relativism that concerns whether something is true or false relative to a framework.

questions_to_think_about: If two people disagree about a food’s taste, must one of them be wrong?
Does learning about different cultures show that all values are relative?
Can people be tolerant without believing that every value is relative?
If all truths were relative, would relativism itself be relative?

summaries.example: Suppose one student says, “The film is brilliant,” while another says, “The film is boring.” A simple subjectivist reading treats these as reports about the speakers’ reactions. A contextualist might say each statement is true relative to the speaker’s standards. A truth-relativist might instead hold that both speakers are discussing one proposition—whether the film is brilliant—but that its truth can vary with a context of assessment. This is meant to preserve both genuine disagreement and the possibility that neither speaker has made an ordinary mistake.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents relativism as a group of related positions rather than a single doctrine. At a high level, a relativist holds that at least some properties—being true, justified, morally right, beautiful, or rational—depend on a framework of assessment. The framework may be an individual standpoint, a culture, a historical period, a language, a conceptual scheme, or an assessor’s standards. The co-variance approach asks two questions: what is being relativized, and what is it being relativized to? A contrasting approach defines relativism by rejecting absolutism, objectivism, or monism—the view that every disputed question has only one correct answer. The hidden-parameter approach says that a claim such as “action A is right” may be incomplete until we specify “right according to framework C.” The scope of relativism matters. Global relativism applies to all beliefs, whereas local relativism concerns only selected domains. Strong relativism says that one judgment may be true in one framework and false in another; weak relativism says that some claims may be available only from certain perspectives. The entry surveys motivations for relativism, including cultural diversity, apparently intractable disagreement, the absence of neutral standards, underdetermination of theories by evidence, and the role of social context. It also explains why critics question whether relative truth is coherent, whether relativism can preserve disagreement and communication, and whether tolerance follows from it. More recent “New Relativism” uses a context of assessment to explain how one proposition might be true for one assessor and false for another without making either speaker simply mistaken.
key_ideas: Relativism can be defined positively through dependence on a framework, negatively through rejection of absolutism or objectivism, or semantically through a hidden parameter.

The object and domain of relativization must be distinguished: one may relativize truth, morality, beauty, or rationality to individuals, cultures, historical periods, languages, or assessment standards.
Local relativism is more common than global relativism because global relativism appears vulnerable to self-refutation: if everything is relative, relativism may be relative too.
Weak relativism concerns claims that are available or expressible only within a framework; strong relativism allows the same judgment to be true in one framework and false in another.
Relativists appeal to diversity, persistent disagreement, lack of neutral standards, theory underdetermination, context dependence, and tolerance.

Objections include incoherence, difficulty explaining genuine disagreement, problems with cross-framework communication, and the worry that relativism permits excessive intellectual or moral permissiveness.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relativism matters because it challenges the assumption that every important judgment can be assessed from a single, framework-independent standpoint. It can illuminate how language, culture, history, and standards of inquiry shape thought, and it may encourage intellectual humility. Yet it also raises demanding philosophical problems. If standards differ, how can we criticize a framework, learn from another one, or argue that evidence supports a conclusion? If disagreement can be faultless, what remains of disagreement? important_terms.definition: A family of views holding that some properties—such as truth, moral rightness, beauty, or rational justification—belong to things only relative to a framework or parameter.
The claim that a phenomenon varies with an underlying variable, such as a culture, language, conceptual scheme, or standard of assessment.
A possibly unstated factor that must be supplied before a claim is evaluated, such as “true according to framework C.”
The view that some truths or values are universal and independent of historical, cultural, or social frameworks.
The view that truth, value, or rational standards are independent of particular judgments, beliefs, or perspectives.
Relativism restricted to a particular area, such as ethics, aesthetics, taste, or epistemic justification.
The broad claim that all beliefs or truths are relative to some framework.
A stronger view on which the same judgment can be true in one framework and false in another.

questions_to_think_about: Does persistent disagreement support relativism, or could disagreement result from error, different evidence, or different circumstances?
Can a claim be true relative to a framework without merely meaning that people in that framework believe it?
Is a local relativism about taste or morality more defensible than a global relativism about all truth?
Can relativism explain genuine disagreement while allowing both parties to be faultless?
Does respect for cultural difference require philosophical relativism?

summaries.example: Your class is choosing a song for a school event. Maya says the song is exciting, while Leo says it is annoying. Their disagreement may partly depend on their different tastes. A philosopher could ask whether “exciting” is true for one listener, true by a group’s standards, or true in some single way that makes one student mistaken. This small example shows why philosophers discuss standards, points of view, and disagreement.
summaries.summary: Relativism is the name for a range of philosophical ideas about dependence on viewpoints or standards. In its simplest form, it says that something may be true, right, beautiful, or reasonable only relative to a framework. A framework could be an individual’s preferences, a culture’s customs, a language, a historical period, or a system for deciding what counts as evidence. The entry explains three related ways of identifying relativism. The first looks at co-variation: if the framework changes, the judgment may change too. The second defines relativism by contrast with absolutism, objectivism, and monism. The third says that ordinary claims may hide a parameter: “This is right” may really mean “This is right according to standard C.” Relativism also differs in scope. Global relativism says everything is relative, while local relativism applies only to particular areas. Strong relativism says one judgment may be true in one framework and false in another. Weak relativism says that some ideas can be understood or expressed only within a particular way of life. The entry describes reasons people find relativism attractive, including cultural diversity, long-lasting disagreements, the possibility that no neutral standard exists, and the influence of social context. Critics argue that relativism may be self-refuting, make disagreement hard to explain, or allow too much. The entry presents these disputes without treating every form of relativism as identical.
key_ideas: Relativism is a broad label for several views about truth, values, knowledge, and reasoning.
A relativist asks both what depends on something else and what it depends on.
Some philosophers describe relativism as rejecting universal standards or the idea that there is one correct answer in every dispute.
A claim can be understood as having an unstated ending, such as “true according to this culture” or “right by this moral code.”
Local relativism makes a limited claim; global relativism makes a much broader claim and faces worries about self-refutation.
Relativists and their critics disagree about whether diversity and disagreement show that there are several valid standards or merely that some people are mistaken.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relativism matters in everyday life because people often meet different customs, opinions, and ways of explaining the world. It can remind us that our own standards are not automatically the only possible standards. But it does not settle every disagreement. Philosophers ask whether some standards can still be better justified, whether different groups can communicate, and whether tolerance itself can be a universal value. Thinking about relativism can make us more careful: we can listen to other viewpoints while still asking for reasons and evidence.

important_terms.definition: The view that some answers depend on a person, group, culture, language, or other way of judging.
A set of ideas or rules used to judge something, such as whether a belief is true or an action is right.
The claim that some truths or values are universal rather than dependent on a particular framework.
The idea that a judgment is correct only when a relevant standard, such as a culture or point of view, is supplied.
Relativism limited to one subject area, such as taste, morality, or science.
Relativism that applies to every belief or subject area.
A disagreement in which each side may be correct according to its own standard.

questions_to_think_about: When people disagree, does that show that truth depends on a viewpoint?
What is the difference between respecting a person’s view and saying that the view is correct?
Could a culture have different values without every member sharing exactly the same beliefs?
Would a global relativist be able to claim that global relativism is true?
Can two people genuinely disagree if both are correct by their own standards?
